grammar.title: Yes/no questions
grammar.rule: Any question someone could answer with yes or no gets raised eyebrows, wide eyes and a slight forward lean of the head. Hold that face from the first sign to the last, and hold the last sign a beat.
grammar.tip: Ending with YOU (pointing at the person again) makes the question feel natural.

clips.cap: Dr. Bill Vicars on raising your brows for a yes/no question
Dr. Bill Vicars: a yes/no question that repeats YOU at the end

drills.en: Do you want to go to a movie tomorrow?

grammar.title: WH-questions
grammar.rule: Who, what, where, when, why, which and how questions get lowered, squeezed eyebrows and a small head tilt. The WH-sign usually comes at the end of the question.
grammar.tip: Raised brows on a WH-question changes it into a rhetorical question, so keep them down when you really want an answer.

clips.cap: Dr. Bill Vicars signs HOW ARE YOU?
Dr. Bill Vicars: WHY with brows down vs. brows up

drills.en: How many children do you have?
Which do you prefer, coffee or tea?

grammar.title: Saying no
grammar.rule: Shake your head side to side while you sign the part you're negating, usually with a slight frown. The head shake carries the meaning: it can make a sentence negative even without the sign NOT.
grammar.tip: Start the shake with the first negated sign and stop when the negated part ends.

clips.cap: Dr. Bill Vicars signs NONE / NOTHING

drills.en: I've never been to the beach.

grammar.title: Topic first
grammar.rule: ASL often names what you're talking about first, with raised brows and a tiny pause, then says something about it with a neutral face. Think: "Pizza? I love it."
grammar.tip: The pause after the topic is short, about as long as a comma.

grammar.title: Rhetorical questions
grammar.rule: Ask a WH-question with your brows up (not down), then answer it yourself. It works like "because" or "so" in English, and it keeps the person watching.
grammar.tip: Raised brows tell the person not to answer, because you're about to.

clips.cap: Mary doesn't like her job. Why? The pay is low.
The teacher is frustrated. Why? The students talk too much.
My sister gave away her old furniture. Why? She moved into a new house.
My worst class is government. Why? The teacher is boring.
My uncle is strong. Why? He works on a farm every day.
I don't like winter. Why? It gets dark early.
Elaine doesn't want to go boating. Why? She's afraid of water.

drills.en: I'm tired because I worked all day.
I went to the store to buy milk.
I'm learning ASL so I can chat with Deaf friends.
She's happy because tomorrow is her birthday.

grammar.title: If… then
grammar.rule: Raise your brows during the condition ("if it rains tomorrow"), pause, then drop to a neutral face for the result. You can sign IF or SUPPOSE at the start, but the face alone can do the job.
grammar.tip: The brow drop is the "then". Make the switch clear.

clips.cap: Dr. Bill Vicars signs IF / SUPPOSE

drills.en: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home.
If you don't understand, ask the teacher.
If you see my brother, tell him hello.

grammar.title: Mouth shapes
grammar.rule: Small mouth shapes add meaning to a sign the way adverbs and adjectives do in English. These seven turn up constantly.
grammar.tip: The mouth shape happens at the same moment as the sign, not before or after it.

shapes.name: MM
shapes.how: Lips pressed together and pushed out a little.

shapes.name: OO
shapes.how: Lips rounded and pursed, like saying "oo".

shapes.name: CHA
shapes.how: Mouth opens with a "cha" as the sign lands.

shapes.name: CS
shapes.how: Teeth together, lips pulled back, head tilted to the shoulder.

shapes.name: TH
shapes.how: Tongue resting slightly between the teeth.

shapes.name: PUFF
shapes.means: a lot, many, a huge amount

shapes.name: PAH
shapes.how: Lips burst open as the sign moves.
